references.text: The angel of the Lord finds Hagar in the wilderness for the first time and speaks to her about Ishmael—a direct parallel to God's angel calling out to Hagar from heaven in 21:17.
God assures Abraham that Ishmael will also become a nation, underscoring God's care and plan for Ishmael and explaining why God intervenes in verse 17.
The angel of the Lord calls out to Abraham from heaven, a close parallel to God's angel calling out to Hagar from heaven in 21:17.
The righteous cry out, and the Lord hears and delivers them from all their distress—a parallel to how God heard the boy's voice and intervened.
God says He has seen the suffering of His people and heard their cry, reflecting how God heard Ishmael's voice and acted to save them.
God fulfills the desires of those who fear Him and hears their cries, as reflected in how God responded to Ishmael's weeping.
Confirms the theological theme of God's ability to hear and answer cries in distress.
Highlights God's angels as active agents in carrying out God's promises and protecting His people.
Parallel in English message: 'Do not be afraid' combined with confirmation that God has heard a prayer.
Direct continuation of the same story: God's angels confirm that He has heard Hagar and Ishmael.
Theological parallel: God's ability to hear and answer cries in distress.
Parallel in English affirmation: Prayers and cries are heard by God.
Theological parallel: God as refuge and help in times of trouble.
Theological parallel: God as good and a refuge on the day of trouble.
Contrast between doubt (Job) and confirmation (Hagar) regarding God's ability to hear in distress.
